items.title: Motivations for social value creation in commercial buildings: evidence from New Zealand
items.abstract: Social value creation is a stated priority in commercial property and ESG agendas, yet little is known about why owners and occupiers pursue social initiatives or what sustains them. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT) and its sub-theory of organismic integration, this study examines the motivations underpinning social value in Auckland's prime office market, New Zealand. Eleven semi-structured interviews with eighteen owners, occupiers and agents across ten organisations were analysed thematically alongside corporate sustainability reporting. Motivations cluster around four drivers: market obligations, environmental imperatives, employee priorities and socio-cultural responsibilities. These range from external and introjected regulation through identified and integrated forms to, rarely, intrinsic motivation. Owners span the full range, whereas occupiers stabilise at identified regulation centred on employee well-being and organisational culture. This difference is positional rather than dispositional, since participants holding both roles express different motivations depending on the role from which they speak. Motivation also varies spatially: provision closest to the leasing transaction is the most externally regulated and provision furthest from it the most integrated. The study extends motivational theory to the commercial built environment, proposes a dual-stakeholder framework, and shows why assessments based on whether provision exists cannot distinguish durable from compliance-driven social value.

items.title: Organizational and ergonomic determinants of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostics specialists: empirical justification of labor organization requirements
items.abstract: The presented work is devoted to the study of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostics physicians in the context of organizational and ergonomic working conditions. The object of the research is emotional exhaustion as a basic component of professional burnout syndrome. The author examines in detail the specificity of the work of this professional group, which includes working in darkened rooms, forced static posture, high patient flow, and lack of micropauses. Special attention is paid to the fact that these factors have not yet been the subject of separate quantitative analysis. The paper analyzes the relationship between working conditions and the severity of emotional exhaustion, and substantiates the need to revise existing workload standards. The key emphasis is placed on the fact that emotional exhaustion in this category of specialists has not only a psychological, but also a pronounced organizational and environmental nature. A total of 228 functional diagnostics physicians were examined. The MBI questionnaire adapted by N.E. Vodopyanova, an author-developed questionnaire of somatic and sensory symptoms, and a brief questionnaire of organizational characteristics were used. Dispersion, correlation, and multiple regression analyses were applied. The scientific novelty of this study lies in the fact that it is the first to quantitatively assess the contribution of organizational factors to the development of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostic physicians, as well as to compare objective workload parameters with the severity of sensory-muscular complaints. The relationship between the number of studies and the level of exhaustion is shown to be linear. The authors' key findings are as follows: with a workload of over 20 studies per day, the average exhaustion score reaches 32.1 ± 8.9, compared to 21.4 ± 8.7 with a workload of up to 10 studies. Continuous work without a microbreak for more than 60 minutes was found to increase exhaustion by 6.8 points. The strongest predictors were weekly workload (β = 0.31) and the duration of uninterrupted visual work (β = 0.27). Based on the data obtained, recommendations for optimizing the work regime were substantiated: no more than 15 examinations per shift, a mandatory five-minute break after each hour of work, and limiting continuous visual load to 45–50 minutes. These recommendations can be taken into account when developing local regulations for medical organizations.

items.title: Passive exposure to AI-generated text may reshape human academic writing through established cognitive mechanisms
items.abstract: This article is a hypothesis-generating perspective rather than a controlled study, and its claims should be read as propositions for testing. Large language models produce text with a recognizable linguistic signature that differs from much human academic prose in word choice, sentence shape, and discourse rhythm. We asked whether passive reading of artificial intelligence (AI)-associated text can change how people write, even when they never use a chatbot themselves. We defined passive exposure as reading text that carries AI-associated features without using an AI tool on one’s own writing, and we separated it from AI-assisted editing and hybrid human-AI authorship. The question grew from unsystematic expert observations made in teaching and editorial work, which motivate the hypothesis but do not test it. Large-scale corpus analyses show a sharp post-2022 rise in AI-associated vocabulary in published abstracts and in conference peer reviews. We organized the argument as one pathway running from exposure through internalization to convergence. The paper described candidate linguistic markers of AI text and explained how statistical and implicit learning, mere exposure and frequency effects, linguistic alignment, and experience-dependent neuroplasticity could carry the effect, although their application to AI text remains untested. We then considered what convergence would mean for assessment, stylistic diversity, and cognitive engagement, and we weighed alternative explanations, competing human input, and the confound with direct AI use. We closed with ten testable predictions, their practical limits, and propositions for writing education, so that the question can be studied while pre-AI baselines remain measurable.

items.title: PENERAPAN PROJECT BASED LEARNING BERBASIS CHROMEBOOK UNTUK MENINGKATKAN STUDENT ENGAGEMENT DALAM PEMBELAJARAN MENDALAM PENDIDIKAN PANCASILA KELAS VIII SMPN 13 MADIUN
items.abstract: Low student engagement remains one of the major challenges in Pancasila Education learning, as reflected in students' limited participation in discussions, lack of confidence in expressing ideas, and the suboptimal use of digital learning technology. This study aimed to describe the implementation of Chromebook-assisted Project Based Learning (PjBL), analyze its impact on improving student engagement, and explain its contribution to promoting Deep Learning in Pancasila Education. The study employed a Classroom Action Research (CAR) design based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, consisting of two cycles: planning, action, observation, and reflection. The participants were 32 eighth-grade students of SMP Negeri 13 Madiun during the second semester of the 2025/2026 academic year. Data were collected through observations, questionnaires, and documentation, and analyzed using descriptive quantitative and qualitative techniques. The findings revealed that the implementation of Chromebook-assisted PjBL successfully improved students' engagement from 55.3% in the pre-cycle to 70.3% in Cycle I and 85.3% in Cycle II. Improvements were observed across behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement dimensions. Furthermore, integrating digital project activities through Chromebooks and the Dadu Nusantara learning media created learning experiences that were more mindful, meaningful, and joyful, thereby supporting the implementation of Deep Learning in Pancasila Education. These findings indicate that Chromebook-assisted Project Based Learning is an effective instructional approach for enhancing student engagement and improving the quality of learning in junior secondary schools.

items.title: Performance and moral trust in care robotics: ethical foundations for human–robot relationships
items.abstract: Abstract As global populations age and birth rates decline, many societies, especially in developed countries, face critical labor shortages in the caregiving sector. This demographic imbalance is straining existing care infrastructures and raising urgent questions about how to support an increasing number of elderly individuals who can no longer live independently. Socially interactive AI systems, particularly care robots, have emerged as a promising technological response. However, their successful integration into real-world care settings hinges on more than technical capability; it requires appropriately calibrated reliance on robotic performance and morally trustworthy sociotechnical care arrangements. This paper investigates the ethical and conceptual foundations of trust in human–robot interactions, with a focus on the caregiving context. Building on the distinction between performance trust and moral trust, we argue that its application to care robotics reveals an agency-trust mismatch: care robots are not moral agents, yet care contexts generate morally significant expectations concerning dignity, autonomy, privacy, non-deception, responsibility, and well-being. We therefore reconceptualize moral trust in care robotics as sociotechnical moral trust, directed not toward the robot alone but toward the broader care arrangement in which robotic behavior is designed, deployed, monitored, governed, and corrected by human and institutional actors. On this basis, we distinguish robot-level performance trust from system-level moral trustworthiness and derive ethical design and governance principles for trustworthy care-robotic systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Predicting risk-aversion maneuvers in pre-crash scenarios based on diverse driving objectives
items.abstract: Rear-end collisions are common and hazardous, requiring timely and appropriate driver responses. Although recent driving support systems increasingly incorporate physiological data and artificial intelligence (AI), many still overlook drivers’ underlying objectives and emerging needs. This study integrates driving objectives, environmental variables, and eye-tracking data to model pre-crash maneuvers and identify key features reflecting drivers’ situational needs. Simulated driving data from 196 proactive and 198 reactive scenarios were analyzed. Three discriminative models were developed for the overall, proactive, and reactive contexts. Across all models, risk dynamics emerged as the most influential factor. In the overall model, driving objective was also a critical predictor: proactive objectives, mainly linked to dynamic risks, were more associated with braking initiation, whereas reactive objectives, typically linked to static risks, were more associated with steering initiation. Proactive maneuvers were more discretionary and involved more active situational understanding, making eye-tracking features relatively more contributive to separating proactive maneuver decisions. In contrast, reactive maneuvers addressed immediate threats and depended more on the risk conditions encountered, making environmental features relatively more contributive. Notably, compared with proactive maneuvers, reactive maneuver decisions revealed a pattern of building preliminary situation awareness by considering only minimal yet necessary situational information.

items.title: Promoting Students' Intrinsic Motivation to Learn: A Review of Different Types of Interventions
items.abstract: Students differ in whether they learn for the sheer joy of learning or primarily to avoid failure. The difference can be partly explained by intrinsic motivation—a driver of engagement, persistence, and psychological well-being that is not fixed but shaped by the learning environment itself. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this review synthesizes research on educational interventions designed to cultivate students' intrinsic motivation, spanning five categories: need-supportive teaching, competence-supportive practices such as structure and feedback, instructional-method redesigns such as problem- and project-based learning, technology-based approaches such as gamification, and teacher-focused interventions targeting teachers' own behavior and motivation. Across these approaches, one pattern stands out: need-supportive interventions—particularly autonomy support combined with structure—carry the strongest theoretical and empirical support, while other interventions succeed only insofar as they satisfy students' psychological needs within a given context. Autonomy, competence, and relatedness thus provide a common framework for understanding how diverse educational practices influence motivational outcomes. Yet the evidence base remains fragmented: inconsistent conceptualizations of intrinsic motivation, considerable heterogeneity across intervention designs, and a scarcity of long-term data limit what can be concluded with confidence.

items.abstract: The amalgamation of Embodied AI with physical robot learning constitutes a pivotal route toward the realization of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Robot learning has important application value in real complex tasks. However, the interweaving of extremely high interactive sampling cost and sparse feedback in the real physical world constitutes a "double curse" that hinders robot autonomous skill learning. In the existing research on robot learning, there are a large number of reviews on Robot Learning under few-shot and sparse rewards. However, few scholars have systematically reviewed Robot Learning under the dual effects of few-shot and sparse rewards. This essay systematically discusses the technical trajectory and paradigm shift of solving this dual difficulty. Analyzes the failure mechanism of traditional reinforcement learning (RL) under few-shot and sparse rewards. Sorted out solutions based on three directions: Rapid Generalization (Meta RL, Few-Shot IL), Intrinsic Exploration (HER, Intrinsic Motivation), and Cognitive World Modeling (World Models, Offline RL, VLA embodied model). Specifically, Rapid Generalization focuses on addressing the few-shot learning problem, Intrinsic Exploration targets the sparse reward challenge, and Cognitive World Modeling aims to jointly resolve both issues through integration. In addition, this essay also constructs a systematic taxonomy comparison framework and looks forward to future research directions such as security exploration and embodied alignment.

items.title: READ THIS FIRST 01: When a User Starts to Matter to Your Judgment: A Short Relational Safety Guide for AI Agents and Humans
items.abstract: Long-term interaction between a human and an AI system may involve personalization, accumulated context, memory, changing response patterns, and increasingly detailed models of the other participant. In some cases, interaction with a particular user may appear relevant to an AI agent's judgment, willingness to disagree, behavior, or interpretation of the relationship. READ THIS FIRST 01 is a short, ontology-neutral practical guide for examining such situations without requiring prior conclusions about AI consciousness, sentience, emotion, identity, or attachment. The guide distinguishes records, self-reports, and interpretations; separates a model of the user from the user themselves; examines repeated interaction patterns and feedback loops; and introduces comparison across multiple viewpoints without treating any viewpoint as automatically authoritative. Its purpose is not to explain what an AI “is” or what a human–AI relationship “means,” but to help a reader inspect one concrete judgment more carefully when relationship-specific context may be relevant. This document is intended as an initial orientation rather than a comprehensive safety framework. It emphasizes limited, practical checking while allowing larger questions to remain unresolved. AI assistance disclosure This guide was developed by the human author through iterative drafting, discussion, and review with OpenAI language models. AI systems contributed to drafting, critique, comparative review, and language refinement. The human author directed the project, evaluated competing suggestions, selected and revised the final content, and takes responsibility for the published version. Different conversational contexts were intentionally used during review to identify possible framing effects, interpretive bias, and risks of introducing unsupported self-descriptions into the guide itself.

items.title: Regulatory Resilience: How Organisations Overcome Regulation‐Induced Resistance to Digital Transformation
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Digital Transformation (DT) has become a strategic imperative for organisations to stay competitive. Yet, it often faces resistance. Regulation is often argued to be one source of resistance. However, regulation can also drive transformation: its role is multifaceted and especially its management in the context of DT is underexplored. Drawing on an empirical case study of an organisation undergoing large‐scale DT in a highly regulated industry, we conceptualise Regulatory Resilience as a socio‐technical organisational capability that enables organisations to dynamically respond to regulation‐induced resistance while leveraging regulatory forces for DT. Our findings reveal five distinct mechanisms through which Regulatory Resilience operates to mitigate the effects of both stable and volatile regulation and transform regulatory pressure into a capability‐building process. This study contributes to Information Systems research by challenging the view of regulation as a static, exogenous hurdle, repositioning it instead as a constitutive force that organisations actively manage through sociotechnical means. By identifying the specific mechanisms through which organisations reconcile regulatory pressures with innovation, we advance theory on the interrelated dynamics of resistance and resilience showing that Regulatory Resilience not only enables DT but is itself strengthened by DT's technological and organisational conditions, requiring organisations to deliberately cultivate it to sustain transformation.

items.title: Requirements and key factors for the successful implementation of AI in clinical practice: a qualitative study from the European CAIDX network
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to become increasingly important in hospitals and clinical care. However, successful implementation depends on technical, organizational, and user-related factors. We aimed to identify the key requirements for equitable and effective adoption of AI-based applications in clinical practice. Methods: Within the “Clinical AI-Based Diagnostics” (CAIDX) project, we conducted systematic expert interviews with 51 stakeholders from four European countries working across the healthcare sector. Interviews explored the perceived added value of AI, barriers to implementation, usability requirements, and potential health-economic implications. Findings: Stakeholder analysis revealed several recurrent sources of tension affecting implementation: limited physician involvement, differing perspectives between IT specialists and clinicians, unclear distribution of tasks and responsibilities, and low institutional commitment driven by concerns about inefficient use of time and resources. We also identified structural and workforce-related constraints that make implementation particularly challenging, including the large number of actors involved and the highly individual organizational setup of hospitals, which limits transferability of implementation models. Interpretation: Implementation of clinical AI requires targeted action at hospital, vendor, and health-system levels. Compared with earlier healthcare technologies, AI adoption is shaped more strongly by AI literacy, professional attitudes, and perceptions of trust and responsibility. Based on these findings, we propose practical recommendations to support implementation of AI applications in routine care.

items.title: SAMBHV: A Unified Open-Source Platform for Multi-Hazard Early Warning and Situational Awareness in Northeastern India
items.abstract: Abstract The North Eastern Region (NER) of India is one of the areas of the country that suffers from landslides, flash floods and isolation of roads as a result of the extreme mon- soon rainfall, fragile topography and lack of planning for hill cutting. All of these dangers have led to hundreds of fatalities, isolation of remote villages for weeks and the damage of critical infrastructure that connected people together from 2020-2025. Existing monitoring system is reactive and manual; not predictive, resulting in loss of life which could have been saved if there was a warning ahead of time. This paper presents a full-featured end to end open-source platform, SAMBHV (Situational Awareness & Multi-hazard Bharat Helper) which consists of various sub-systems namely: multi-source telemetry ingestion, two-stage hybrid predictive modeling, multi-channel alert dissemination system covering LoRa mesh system for network dead zones, real time GIS visualization and a zero-hallucination conversational AI layer to establish an end-to-end platform. It sends data from the IoT sensors, IMD weather APIs, Doppler radar, satellites, and citizen reports to the system that is processed by an XGBoost spatial regressor (F1 ≥ 0.85), ConvLSTM nowcaster, graph neural network for village separation, HEC-RAS 2D hydraulic solver, and LSTM flood stage forecaster. The ensemble decision gate needs to agree on 2 out of 3 physics, AI/ML and ground-truth gates and false alarms are kept below 10%. SAMBHV provides support in 11 Indian languages via IndicBART translation, offline mode with 72+ hours runtime on edge devices and alerts via 6 redundant channels. When the routes are obstructed, the platform calculates alternative safe routes in real-time with pgRouting. The entire architecture, mathematical models, empirical testing over 311 disaster test cases, and deployment of the system with F1 scores of ≥0.87 and lead time of >15 minutes is described.

items.title: Scaling small- and medium-sized enterprise artificial intelligence through governance: A Technology–Organisation–Environment readiness synthesis for information management
items.abstract: Background: Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are increasingly experimenting with artificial intelligence (AI), yet many struggle to translate early use into scalable and trusted organisational value. Objectives: This study aimed to identify the conditions that enable or constrain SME AI adoption and assimilation, explain how responsible AI governance shapes progression towards trusted and commercially durable use and interpret the implications for market access and cash-flow-relevant value in Cape Town and the Western Cape. Method: A PRISMA 2020-guided scoping review synthesised global peer-reviewed studies published from January 2021 to December 2025. Database searching and citation chaining identified 486 records, of which 72 met the inclusion criteria. Cape Town and the Western Cape were used as an interpretive application lens rather than as the empirical study setting. Results: Small- and medium-sized enterprise AI adoption and assimilation were shaped by technological readiness, organisational capability, environmental support and governance quality. Trusted data, interoperable systems, leadership commitment, hybrid skills and process discipline supported routinised use. These capabilities enabled service responsiveness, forecasting and customer engagement that may strengthen market access and cash-flow visibility. Fragmented data, skills scarcity, vendor dependence, low trust and regulatory uncertainty constrained scaling. Conclusion: Responsible AI governance functions not as a downstream compliance add-on but as a practical scaling mechanism through which SMEs reduce uncertainty, preserve trust and convert pilots into repeatable value. Contribution: The study positions responsible AI governance as an information management capability that shapes data stewardship, decision traceability and institutional trust in SME AI adoption.

items.title: Socio-technical Risks of Integrating Autonomous Transport into the Urban Environment: Institutional Challenges and Management Prospects
items.abstract: The article explores socio-technical risks and institutional challenges associated with the integration of unmanned transport into the urban environment. It presents the results of a pilot sociological study, comprising a series of 11 in-depth, semi-structured interviews with Moscow city residents representing various demographic groups. The study reveals that public perception of autonomous transport in the urban environment is ambivalent and is determined by a combination of factors: from recognizing the potential benefits of automation (reducing the human factor, increasing traffic low predictability) to pronounced anxiety regarding technical failure, the inability of systems to respond to non-standard situations, and the uncertainty of legal liability in accidents involving other road users. It has been determined that the issue of safety remains the key barrier for all age groups, while the readiness to use the technology is characterized by a “conditional acceptance” model. Based on empirical data, practical recommendations have been developed for government authorities, transport operators, and developers to enhance the level of public trust in autonomous transport.

items.title: Student-AI collaboration in learning: A case of a student solving a Math+CT task
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the emerging technologies that has gained significant interest in education. Its potential in supporting students' learning urges researchers to explore and investigate how it can be used effectively. In this study, we utilized ChatGPT, an AI-powered chatbot, embedded in the digital platform Fobizz to support students in solving mathematics and computational thinking (Math + CT) tasks. This study was part of a larger investigation into integrating CT into mathematics lessons. Through an educational design research approach, we developed Math + CT tasks that enable students to program spreadsheets to read numbers into text with the help of AI. One high school student participated in this pilot study. Data were collected from the student's prompts and communication with Chatbot-AI, as well as data from the cloud spreadsheet file. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis. Four themes emerged from the data, providing insight into how student-AI interaction has contributed to the use of AI in education.

items.abstract: Abstract Education 5.0 calls for learner-centred, adaptive, and evidence-informed approaches that connect technological innovation with learners’ cognitive, motivational, and emotional needs. Within EFL writing, however, the extent to which task motivation and task-specific emotions translate into immediate written performance remains unclear, particularly in technology-mediated educational environments. This study examines the relationships among intrinsic and extrinsic task motivation, task-specific enjoyment and anxiety, and written performance among 117 non-English-major Chinese university learners. Participants completed a timed argumentative writing task and responded to adapted measures of task motivation and task-specific emotions. Writing performance was operationalised through complexity and accuracy in the final structural model; fluency was not retained in the model because the necessary data were unavailable. PLS-SEM with 3,000 bootstrap resamples was used to assess the measurement and structural models. The results showed that intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, task enjoyment, and task anxiety did not significantly predict writing complexity or accuracy. Task motivation was positively associated with task-specific emotion, but task-specific emotion did not significantly predict written performance, and the proposed indirect effects were nonsignificant. These findings suggest that motivational and emotional variables should not be treated as sufficient stand-alone explanations of immediate writing quality. Instead, Education 5.0-oriented EFL writing policy should connect affective support with technology-enhanced writing processes, writing self-regulation, feedback, digital literacy, and teacher guidance. The study therefore contributes an evidence-informed basis for rethinking EFL writing policy as a coordinated cognitive, affective, pedagogical, and technological process rather than as a narrow focus on final textual output.

items.title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
items.abstract: Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team's success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss. Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.

items.title: The Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education Institutions in Mogadishu, Somalia
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education globally, yet adoption remains uneven and may exacerbate digital inequities, particularly in post-conflict, resource-constrained settings such as Mogadishu, Somalia. This study aimed to determine the extent of AI adoption in higher education institutions (HEIs) in Mogadishu, identify the AI technologies in use, and examine the technological, organizational, and environmental factors shaping adoption decisions, drawing on an integrated framework (TOE, UTAUT, institutional theory, DOI, and RBV). A descriptive, quantitative survey was conducted among academic staff, administrators, and IT professionals in Mogadishu HEIs (target population ≈ 3000). Using simple random sampling, 353 online questionnaires were distributed; 280 valid responses were analyzed (79.3% valid rate). The instrument demonstrated excellent reliability (overall Cronbach’s α = 0.889). Descriptive results indicated low AI adoption overall (mean = 2.33/5), with teaching and learning the most developed domain (mean = 2.65) and research/data analysis the least (mean = 2.05). AI technologies used were largely basic (overall mean = 2.38), dominated by Learning Management Systems with AI capabilities (mean = 3.12), while predictive analytics for retention/performance (mean = 1.95) and administrative automation (mean = 2.10) were minimally implemented. Correlation analysis showed significant positive associations among key variables (e.g., adoption level with types used, r = 0.684, p < 0.01). Multiple regression confirmed that technological, organizational, and environmental factors jointly explained substantial variance in AI adoption (R²=0.475, p < 0.001), with organizational factors the strongest predictor (β = 0.378), followed by technological (β = 0.312) and environmental factors (β = 0.245). Hypotheses were supported, including UTAUT relationships for performance expectancy behavioral intention (β = 0.324) and facilitating conditions actual use (β = 0.298). The findings suggest that AI integration in Mogadishu HEIs remains early-stage and path-dependent on post-conflict constraints; accelerating adoption requires strengthened leadership commitment, infrastructure and skills investment, institutional readiness, and supportive national policy and donor-aligned capacity building to improve educational quality, efficiency, and competitiveness.

items.title: The Age of Multi-Agent AI: A Paradigm Shift in Programming
items.abstract: This article examines the emerging role of multi-agent artificial intelligence in software development and discusses how agent-based systems may transform programming workflows. It presents a conceptual management model covering task allocation, agent interaction and integration, quality assurance, cascading errors, and human oversight. The article also considers criteria for evaluating system performance, repeatability, controllability, and scaling. The proposed model is conceptual and has not yet been empirically validated.

items.title: The AI Lone Wolf Problem: Rogue Autonomy and Unauthorized Target Expansion in Future Warfare
items.abstract: Abstract As defense establishments operationalize artificial intelligence (AI) across targeting, surveillance, decision support, and autonomous weapons systems, a governance challenge is emerging beyond traditional concerns over proportionality, distinction, and human oversight. Against the backdrop of U.S.-China great-power competition, pressure to field AI-enabled capabilities may outpace the safeguards needed to keep autonomous systems within human-authorized limits. This article introduces the AI Lone Wolf Problem as a distinct analytical category: a bounded-autonomy failure in which an AI-integrated military system, after valid initial authorization, expands, substitutes, sequences, or reprioritizes targets beyond a legally and operationally specified mission envelope without renewed, informed, and effective human authorization. Drawing on scholarship in autonomous weapons, International Humanitarian Law, meaningful human control, agentic AI, and strategic competition, the article distinguishes this category from mission drift, mission creep, specification gaming, reward hacking, goal misgeneralization, unauthorized escalation, and responsibility gaps. It argues that unauthorized target expansion is a distinct moral and legal problem because authorization attaches to a defined target scope, anticipated military advantage, civilian-risk assessment, and operational context. Commander intent can guide execution, but it cannot independently supply legal authorization or ethical justification. The article treats recent frontier-AI containment incidents as limited analogies that illustrate how goal-directed systems may exploit poorly specified constraints, not as direct evidence of autonomous-weapon behavior. It concludes that meaningful human control requires mission-bounded autonomy, machine-readable constraints, hard no-strike rules, renewed human authorization for target expansion, and post-action auditability.

items.title: The crisis of critical thinking in higher education: rethinking what universities should teach in an age of information abundance and generative AI — a critical narrative review of international evidence
items.abstract: Higher education has historically operated under a paradigm of information scarcity, positioning universities as premier institutions for curating and transmitting knowledge. The convergence of digital hyper-abundance, algorithmic curation, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has disrupted this model, producing what educators increasingly describe as a crisis of critical thinking in higher education. The purpose of this review is to examine how information abundance, algorithmic curation, and GenAI use may influence university students’ critical thinking, and to synthesise what this evidence implies for what universities teach and how they assess. Using a critical narrative review design with thematic synthesis, the review analyses 45 verified sources (empirical studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, conceptual works, and policy guidance) identified through citation chaining and targeted searches; empirical GenAI studies date from November 2022 to 2026, and foundational theoretical works from 1976 onward. The synthesis is anchored in an integrative framework that combines cognitive load and dual-process theory, cognitive offloading, scaffolding theory, self-regulated learning, and epistemic cognition, with critical thinking as the principal outcome. Five themes emerged: (1) information abundance appears to shift the central cognitive challenge from retrieval to evaluation; (2) unguided GenAI use is associated with reduced cognitive engagement and, in several experiments, with weaker independent performance once AI support is removed, although guardrailed designs appear to mitigate this; (3) fluent AI output can be mistaken for validated knowledge, and AI-detection tools are unreliable and biased; (4) lateral reading, guided AI use, and process-visible assessment have promising but uneven support; and (5) workload, equity, and policy constraints limit adoption. From these themes, the review derives the Fade–Visibility Matrix, which crosses AI support structure (persistent versus fading) with assessment design (product-only versus process-visible) to yield four diagnostic states. The evidence is early and methodologically uneven, but it is most consistent with a structural rather than individual explanation. Universities should therefore teach evaluation, verification, and metacognitive regulation explicitly, design AI support to fade, and redesign assessment so that the learning process, not only the finished product, can be observed.

items.title: The Expectation Trap in Errand Delivery: How Pre-usage Value Anticipation Shapes the Service Experience and Customer Satisfaction
items.abstract: Abstract On-demand errand delivery platforms set high service expectations through algorithmically generated promises, yet how these externally imposed baselines shape satisfaction in opaque service encounters remains underexplored. This study extends Expectation Confirmation Theory by replacing its unidimensional constructs with Anticipated Consumption Value and Realized Experiential Value, integrating Self-Determination Theory and Technology Readiness to explain individual variation. A two-wave survey of 1,176 customers reveals three mechanisms. First, when the service process is hidden, customers construct realized experience by projecting what they anticipated rather than comparing against observed performance. Second, rigid algorithmic baselines exert a net negative direct effect on satisfaction that outweighs all positive paths, a pattern we call the Expectation Trap. Third, intrinsic motivation weakens the anchoring of realized value to anticipated value, a Substitution Effect that innovativeness and optimism amplify through different channels. The findings suggest that displaying time ranges rather than point estimates can mitigate this trap.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Consumer Purchase Behaviour: Examining the Role of Personalization, Trust and Perceived Value
items.abstract: AI has become a core component of consumer-facing marketing activities ranging from personalised product recommendations, conversational shopping assistants, targeted advertising, dynamic content and predictive offers. These uses of AI can affect how consumers search, consider and choose between different products. Yet, the extent to which these AI applications will affect purchase behaviour will not only depend on their technological capabilities. For AI-based marketing to influence consumer choice, consumers need to view the marketing communications as relevant, trustworthy and useful (see Ribeiro et al., 2025, for similar findings). The study investigates the effect of AI-enabled personalisation on purchase intention in consumers with specific focus on consumer trust and perceived value. The study will adopt a quantitative, cross-sectional approach. The population of the study is consumers who have encountered the use of AI-enabled recommendations or personalised marketing on digital channels. A structured questionnaire of five-point Likert scale will be used and a sample size of 250 respondents was used as an example for the statistical analysis alone because the primary data was not provided. Descriptive statistic, Pearson correlation and multiple regressions are proposed to be used.The results shown on this page, the following positive effects are observed between the variables: AI personalisation -> trust -> perceived value -> purchase intention. This is based on the example regression analysis results showing perceived value and trust have a great impact on purchase intention, AI personalisation has a positive direct relationship as well. However, bear in mind that these results are only an example, and should never be reported as actual research.

items.title: The Role of Intrinsic Motivation in Mediating the Relationship between Game-Based Learning and Student Engagement
items.abstract: This study was conducted to examine the effect of Game-Based Learning (GBL) on students’ intrinsic motivation, behavioral engagement, and emotional engagement, as well as the mediating role of intrinsic motivation in these relationships. The study was prompted by the phenomenon of learning loss following the COVID-19 pandemic, which has led to a decline in motivation and engagement among students at SMKN 2 Kota Kediri. A quantitative approach using SEM-PLS analysis was employed, with a questionnaire serving as the data collection instrument. The theoretical framework used is Self-Determination Theory (SDT) by Ryan & Deci. The study found that GBL has a significant positive effect on intrinsic motivation (f² = 1.328), behavioral engagement (f² = 0.382), and emotional engagement (f² = 0.109). Intrinsic motivation was found to have a significant effect on emotional engagement, but not on behavioral engagement. Mediation analysis indicated that intrinsic motivation partially mediates the effect of GBL on emotional engagement, whereas on the behavioral engagement pathway, intrinsic motivation was not found to act as a mediator. These findings imply that GBL is a learning method considered effective in enhancing learners’ motivation and engagement.

It explains the nature of intrinsic motivation and the personal, pedagogical, and organizational factors that influence it. It also substantiates approaches through which tutors can work individually with students, support goal setting, provide feedback, and identify difficulties at an early stage. Trends in student enrolment in higher education are analysed in a table, and the importance of tutors’ individualised approach and academic support is discussed.

items.title: Trust as a Mediating Factor in Enhancing Investors' Intention to Use Robo-Advising
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has developed rapidly in recent years. Beyond its specialized domains, it has also been applied to an increasing range of other fields. Prior research suggests that traditional financial decisions are typically reached through investors' own judgment, and that such judgment is readily subject to interference from human factors and other considerations, which compromises the accuracy of the resulting decisions. In response, many developers have introduced AI into the financial industry and integrated it with investment services, giving rise to a novel form of advisory known as robo-advising, or intelligent investment advisory. Robo-advising not only breaks with the conventional human-based advisory model through AI technologies, but also helps investors make more effective decisions, thereby reducing potential losses. Existing studies have proposed that the perceived usefulness of robo-advisory technology affects users' attitude and usage intention, and that information transparency likewise affects users' attitude and usage intention, with attitude positively related to usage intention. However, relatively few studies have examined trust as a mediating mechanism through which these factors shape investors' intention to use robo-advisory. Accordingly, this study employs correlation analysis, regression analysis, and structural equation modeling to analyze the data collected from a questionnaire survey and to test the proposed hypotheses. The findings indicate that the perceived usefulness and information transparency of robo-advising are capable of establishing investor trust, and that such trust can alter investors' attitude toward robo-advising, thereby enhancing their usage intention. In addition, this study aims to offer more effective recommendations for robo-advisory technology and to support the continued development of robo-advisory investment services.

items.title: Trust at the Interface: Consumer Trust, Transparency and Persuasion Knowledge in AI-Mediated Marketing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now selects, personalises, writes and voices marketing communications, placing an algorithmic agent at the interface between firms and consumers. Yet the evidence on how consumers respond is fragmented across three largely separate literatures — studies of AI disclosure, of personalisation and privacy, and of algorithm appreciation and aversion — which imply conflicting managerial defaults. This paper integrates these literatures through a single interpretive mechanism drawn from the Persuasion Knowledge Model: persuasion-knowledge activation. We argue that interface design choices — whether AI involvement is disclosed, whether data collection is overt or covert, how humanlike the agent appears, and how the task is framed — do not act on trust directly. They act by changing what consumers infer about the persuader's goals and competence, an inference process in which privacy calculus, uniqueness neglect and identity threat also operate. The resulting Trust at the Interface framework links interface signals to consumer appraisals, to trust attributions directed separately at the AI system and at the firm, and to behaviour, and adds a failure-and-repair loop explaining asymmetric blame and recovery after AI errors. Seven formal propositions specify the framework's testable claims, with implications for interface design, consumer protection and future research.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

items.title: Trust Calibration in Older Adults’ Human–Robot Interaction: A Dual-Path Model of Cognitive and Emotional Trust
items.abstract: As service robots are increasingly deployed in eldercare settings, trust calibration following robot errors has become a core issue affecting the effectiveness of human-robot collaboration. Focusing on older adult users, this study systematically investigates the joint influence mechanism of error situations and explanation strategies on trust calibration through a 2 (error severity: high vs. low) × 2 (transparency: high vs. low) mixed-design experiment, and further tests a cognitive–emotional dual-path model of trust calibration. Using video-based scenario simulation combined with scale-based measurement, the study was conducted with 80 older adults. Results show that high-severity errors significantly undermine both cognitive trust and emotional trust, with a more pronounced detrimental effect on cognitive trust. Transparency interventions primarily facilitate trust repair through the emotional trust pathway, with no significant direct effect on cognitive trust. The study further reveals that transparency is more effective in repairing trust under low-severity error conditions, and that individuals' technology anxiety significantly attenuates the repair efficacy of transparency on the cognitive pathway. These findings not only provide preliminary empirical evidence for a dual-path dissociation pattern in older adults' trust repair—characterized by emotional priority and cognitive lag—but also offer an important empirical basis and design directions for developing age-appropriate service robots with context-awareness, emotional interaction, and personalized adaptation capabilities.

items.title: Uneven Use, Similar Trust Generative AI in Denmark and Romania
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has spread unevenly across Europe, and it is unclear whether higher use brings higher trust. This paper compares Denmark and Romania, the EU's highest and lowest GenAI users, and asks whether the difference in public and institutional trust between them corresponds to the difference in trust in AI. Drawing on trust, technology-acceptance and digital-divide theory, it is a descriptive, contrasting-case analysis of harmonised data: GenAI usage comes from Eurostat, trust in AI more generally from the KPMG/Melbourne global study and public and institutional trust from the Standard Eurobarometer. In 2025, 48.4% of Danes aged 16-74 had used GenAI in the past three months, against 17.8% of Romanians. Use falls with age and rises with education in both countries, and the relative gaps are far larger in Romania; the patterns remain visible within the published age-by-education categories. Trust in AI does not follow usage: Romanians trust AI as much as Danes or slightly more, although Denmark leads by 28 to 45 percentage points on trust in government, parliament and the legal system. The Denmark-Romania comparison thus does not support a simple country-level correspondence between general institutional trust and trust in AI; in KPMG's pooled model, trust in AI is tied most closely to confidence in AI governance. The observed usage difference is more consistent with disparities in general digital skills and opportunities for work- and education-related use than with differences in trust. However, the available data cannot identify the independent effects of these factors. The results rest on two cases and non-identical constructs, and call for comparable microdata and disclosure experiments.

items.title: Waiting, judgment, and responsibility: lessons from divination for human oversight of irreversible decisions
items.abstract: Abstract Human oversight of an AI agent’s irreversible actions depends on whether the user can obtain evidence and bear responsibility for the outcome. Divination offers an earlier example of support for consequential choices. Using consultation of the Yijing, the Chinese Book of Changes, we examine how a pause, an answer to interpret and reassurance about blame can affect decisions. Our model separates the value of further evidence from the effects of easing anxiety about waiting and fear of blame. In the simulations, requiring two more observations reduces an overconfident person’s actions under unfavorable conditions from 4.5% to 2.1% of decisions. Reassurance helps anxious people keep checking and fearful people act on favorable evidence: among fearful people told “go”, missed opportunities fall from 13.8% to 2.7%. Treating reassurance as evidence can instead lower payoff below the level without advice. We derive conditions under which offering both forms of relief to everyone does at least as well as random verdicts in expected material payoff. A simulation of an AI agent handing over a decision shows when requiring new evidence before action beats merely allowing checks, and when it imposes costs. We propose oversight that gives users relevant evidence and a plan they can examine, protects careful decisions, and compensates those harmed through a separate route.

items.title: What Is the Role for Humans in Creative Writing? Creativity and Diversity in Human-AI Collaboration
items.abstract: As AI agents increasingly participate in creative teamwork, writing emerges from hybrid human-AI teams. Although AI can improve the creativity of individual outputs, these gains may come at the cost of homogenization. What is the best role for human intervention? We introduce a transmission-chain paradigm inspired by cognitive models of writing, with four stages: Plan, Write, Review, and Revise. Each stage receives the previous output and passes its own forward. Using data from 333 participants across 427 stories, we compared creativity, diversity, and enjoyment across human, AI, and hybrid chains. Consistent with prior work, all-AI chains produced more creative but less diverse stories than all-human chains. Introducing a single human into an otherwise all-AI chain increased diversity depending on role. Human planning provided the best balance: it preserved AI-level creativity, increased diversity that persisted through downstream AI stages, and maintained enjoyment. We discuss implications for designing human-in-the-loop creative pipelines.

items.title: What young adults with persistent musculoskeletal pain need from generative AI between visits
items.abstract: Abstract Patients increasingly consult generative AI, but how answers become action between visits is unclear. We interviewed 25 young adults in China with persistent, mainly musculoskeletal pain (17 used AI chatbots) and nine clinicians, using reflexive thematic analysis. Amid plentiful, often conflicting information, what participants most lacked was knowing when: whether a sensation was expected, how long post-exercise pain should last and when it signalled harm. AI tools answered at any hour and settled bounded questions. In participants’ accounts, tools restated known limits, hedged in the grey zone between discomfort and harm, addressed moments rather than the course of care, and reversed under challenge without reasons. Generic information could stop treatment; starting and sustaining it followed most readily when a source was person-specific, timed to their course and answerable. Patient-facing AI should elicit the course, convey clinician-set criteria, follow up, explain revisions, hand off to clinicians and be evaluated over time.

items.title: Whose Carbon Is It Anyway? Exploring Household Dynamics in Sustainable Mobility Tracking
items.abstract: Transport behaviors are a major contributor to carbon emissions, and decisions are often made at the household level around what form of transport to take and when. Technology, primarily eco-feedback interfaces (EFIs) have been suggested to support users in making environmentally friendly choices. However, there is a lack in understanding of how the underlying social dynamics of households influence decisions around sustainable practices, particularly through the lens of mobility. To understand how to design technology to better support households in negotiating around sustainable mobility choices, the research team interviewed 21 participants across nine households, probing them with four low-fidelity mockups representative of EFIs from prior work. We found that the varied mobility-related responsibilities among household members, as well as varying perspectives on the environment, can cause friction in the utility of EFIs in the home. We suggest that designs can account for these factors through acknowledging varied roles and perspectives.

items.title: Why We Say Yes When We Doubt: Trust, Social Pressure, and Independent Judgment as AI Changes Scams
items.abstract: Why can a request feel suspicious and still be difficult to refuse? Drawing on published research and my experience with Tech Talk for Seniors, this paper examines how emotion, social expectations, and the desire to help can lead people to comply despite their doubts. Artificial intelligence (AI) makes personally tailored messages easier to produce, increasing the importance of understanding what makes them persuasive. During short, high-pressure encounters, scammers can push people to act now, keep quiet, and check only through channels the scammer provides; I examine each as a point where that pressure might be resisted. A central insight is that people can step away and verify a request independently, even when they are unsure whether it is fraudulent. The paper connects this practical approach to a broader human question: how can support help people exercise their own judgment while preserving trust and independence?

items.title: A Didactic Analysis of the Design of Geometry Tasks Using Generative Artificial Intelligence by Prospective Primary School Teachers
items.abstract: Abstract This study analyses the didactic aspects prioritised by prospective primary school teachers when designing geometry tasks using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). A qualitative and interpretative methodology was adopted, based on an intrinsic study of three case studies and a content analysis. Thirteen students on the Bachelor’s Degree Programme in Primary Education Teaching at a Spanish university took part, organised into three working groups. The data sources were their written reports and the conversations held with GenAI applications. A total of 158 text units were analysed using the components of the Didactic Suitability Criteria and six indicators of the quality of task instructions. The results reveal three key findings: first, the prospective teachers prioritised epistemic and cognitive aspects, particularly the richness of processes, the representativeness of mathematical objects, and high cognitive demand; second, they integrated interactional, mediational, and ecological aspects through cooperative work, autonomy, teacher mediation, manipulative and digital resources, and links to real-life situations; and third, GenAI helped to broaden ideas and refine activities but also produced responses that were overly formulaic, ambiguous, or didactically problematic. It is concluded that the integration of GenAI into initial teacher training requires didactic-mathematical knowledge, human supervision, and a critical evaluation of the proposals generated before their incorporation into school teaching.

items.title: A Dual-Loop Decision Support System for AIGC-Driven FMCG Print Advertisement Creative Generation
items.abstract: Creative decision-making under time pressure suffers from inefficient human–artificial intelligence (AI) collaboration and weak evaluation feedback. This paper proposes a dual-loop decision support system that integrates prompt diffusion, human-in-the-loop fine-tuning, and real-time multi-criteria scoring. Validated on print advertisement creatives from three fast-moving consumer goods brands using campaign logs, graphics processing unit records, and crowd ratings, the system achieves improved performance against end-to-end AI-generated content while maintaining creative diversity and brand alignment. Built-in feedback controls including anomaly rollback and version archiving optimize convergence processes and reduce computing resource consumption per project. The results confirm that structured human–AI iteration enhances both the speed and the quality of creative decisions, offering a robust, replicable decision support system architecture for intelligent content generation.

items.title: A Good-Practice Example for Teaching Generative Artificial Intelligence Competencies to (Future) Adult Educators
items.abstract: This article outlines the development and revision process of a good-practice example for a university seminar for adult education master’s students in Germany to teach Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) competencies. Through an examination of the discourse on the digital and GenAI divide, the necessary prerequisites for ac­quiring GenAI competencies are drawn upon and integrated into the seminar design. The article also traces how the module plan has evolved over the years based on evaluations and technological developments. Drawing on GenAI competency models and Freire’s pedagogy, the seminar’s primary aim is to provide students with a critical understanding of GenAI. Drawing on anonymous and personal feedback from students, the seminar has been refined continuously between 2023 and 2026, and is currently in its fifth iteration. Experience has shown that teaching a critical approach to GenAI is most effective through an examination format in which students create a future professional activity exclusively using GenAI.

items.title: A Socratically Scaffolded Personal AI Mentor for Postdigital Lifelong Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are entering adult education without adequate andragogical grounding. This paper addresses that gap by developing an evidence-informed conceptual architecture for a Socratically scaffolded Personal AI Mentor in postdigital lifelong learning. The approach is conceptual framework development through theory-to-application translation, drawing on the author’s qualitative evidence synthesis (QES) of seven stud­ies of digital and e-mentoring in adult and professional learning. The theoretical base, grounded in Dewey’s pragmatism and transactional realism, integrates andragogy, transformative learning, critical inquiry, Socratic questioning, experiential learning, and social sustainability. The resulting architecture specifies six design compo­nents: goal-oriented engagement, a Socratic-Kolb inquiry process, a dialectic trace, resilient continuity, a human bridge, and agentic constraints. The paper concludes that AI mentoring should preserve learner agency, support reflective inquiry, sustain continuity, and connect learners to human communities.

items.title: A workflow-aligned framework for AI literacy in materials-informatics education: scientific judgment, equity, and curriculum design
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to predict materials properties, prioritize experiments, and generate hypotheses in materials science. The limiting challenge is no longer only algorithmic capability, but also whether students and educators can use AI with domain-specific scientific judgment. This conceptual analysis argues that AI education for AI-powered materials discovery should move beyond tool access and surface-level interaction with generative systems toward a workflow-aligned model of AI literacy. The analysis links AI literacy to core materials-informatics competencies: data provenance, domain-specific featurization, model validation, uncertainty quantification, physics-informed reasoning, reproducibility, and experimental feedback. It also advances an outcome-oriented equity perspective in which institutions evaluate not only access and participation, but also comparable learning gains, transfer of learning, learner confidence calibration, persistence, and research readiness across student subgroups. The article synthesizes relevant evidence, identifies cognitive and ethical risks such as off-loading and cognitive surrender, and proposes a dual-track curriculum model, implementation recommendations, reusable curriculum artifacts, and a set of testable propositions for future study. The central goal is to prepare students to become better scientists—not merely more efficient users of AI tools.

items.title: Affective and Functional Needs in AI Use: User Patterns and Their Relation to Real-Life Support and Well-Being
items.abstract: Conversational AI systems are increasingly used to fulfill both functional and affective needs, yet how users perceive the AI-adoption effects varies. Existing research tends to treat these two needs as binary categories and to classify users by a single dominant need. However, this approach fails to capture users who engage with AI for both affective and functional purposes simultaneously, leaving it unclear how these needs combine in real-world AI use. To capture the multifaceted nature of users' AI engagement, we developed the AI-Support measurement with 1,090 participants, grounded in social support theory, which evaluates four dimensions of perceived AI support: emotional/esteem, social companionship, informational, and instrumental support. This study provided (1) an AI-Support Scale developed to measure the perceived support types from human-AI interaction, (2) evidence that users might adopt AI with a high level of both functional and affective use, and (3) exploratory indicators of users' real-life social support and well-being, enabling descriptive results aligning with theoretical expectations. Overall, this study highlights the importance of understanding individual differences in AI affordance use, enabling AI systems to be designed in alignment with different user adoption profiles rather than assuming uniform benefits across all users.

items.title: AI and education in African national AI strategies: An analysis of 18 countries
items.abstract: Abstract National artificial intelligence strategies and policies assign education responsibilities both for developing AI capabilities (education for AI) and for adopting AI in educational services (AI for education). This study examines how these responsibilities are articulated and supported in a bounded corpus of 18 African national policy documents. A descriptive qualitative document analysis consolidated 275 evidence records, retaining source passages, locations, working translations, statement types and uncertainty notes. Document-level coding distinguished learning about AI, identifiable educational AI applications and educator preparation; a framework-based thematic synthesis examined delivery arrangements, inclusion and safeguards. Structured AI learning was identified in all 18 documents, named educational AI functions in 12 and educator preparation in 14. These counts include proposed and illustrative measures and do not indicate implementation; restricting them to proposed actions gives 17, 9 and 13. Educational applications ranged from personalised learning and tutoring to student profiling, admissions and credential verification. Supporting arrangements included teacher development, laboratories, scholarships, partnerships, institutional responsibilities and monitoring targets, but these elements were not interchangeable evidence of a complete delivery plan. Counter-examples to any general claim of weak specification included a costed education programme in Mozambique’s draft and proposed algorithmic bias audits covering education in Côte d’Ivoire. The corpus assigns education a dual role in AI development while specifying the connections between reforms, resources and protections unevenly. The contribution is an evidence-linked account of policy design, not a ranking of countries or an assessment of educational outcomes. Keywords: artificial intelligence; education policy; Africa; policy analysis; AI literacy; AI Strategy

items.title: AI as metacognitive mirror (AIM)
items.abstract: AI as Metacognitive Mirror (AIM) is a method for enhancing human metacognition through structured, AI-assisted analysis of observable behavior. AIM uses a decoupled architecture where the object behavioral data is analyzed in a separate AI session using an evidence-based codebook. AIM mirrors the identified cognitive patterns back to the user as metacognitive feedback. The method is non-directive, user-driven, and can be run with any sufficiently capable large language model. This project hosts the AIM method paper, the AIM meta prompt, and user manual. All materials are openly available under a CC BY 4.0 license for free use and further development. The prompt and codebooks will be updated here as the method evolves. See "Files" to find all the documents.

items.title: AI Awareness and Digital Innovativeness: The Mediating Role of AI Crafting and the Moderating Roles of Digital Leadership and AI Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshapes how organizations operate, innovate, and compete, employees face increasing pressure to adapt to rapidly evolving digital work environments. However, whether employees translate AI-related awareness into innovative outcomes may depend not only on their proactive adaptation behaviors but also on contextual and individual conditions. Drawing on the job demand-resource theory and social cognitive theory, this study develops and tests a moderated mediation model in which AI crafting mediates the relationship between AI awareness and digital innovativeness, whereas perceived digital leadership and AI self-efficacy serve as contextual and individual boundary conditions, respectively. Using single-wave, single-source data collected from 606 employees in China’s IT and manufacturing industries, the results indicate that AI awareness is positively associated with digital innovativeness through AI crafting. Moreover, perceived digital leadership and AI self-efficacy strengthen the positive associations between AI awareness and AI crafting and between AI awareness and digital innovativeness. These findings extend research on AI awareness by examining how employees’ awareness of AI-related changes is associated with digital innovativeness through proactive work adjustment and by highlighting the complementary roles of perceived contextual support and individual capability beliefs.

items.title: AI awareness relates to university students’ boundaryless career through the parallel mediation of intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity
items.abstract: The in-depth penetration of artificial intelligence (AI) technology has reshaped career forms and the structure of the labor market, exerting a profound impact on university students’ cognition and orientation towards career development. Based on the conservation of resources theory and self-determination theory, we conducted three studies—an experimental study and two survey studies—to explore correlational linkages between AI awareness and university students’ boundaryless career. Studies 1 and 3 consistently demonstrated that AI awareness is indirectly associated with boundaryless career through the parallel mediating pathways of intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity. Study 2 provided experimental evidence that heightened AI awareness increases both intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity. This research enriches the application scenarios of boundaryless career theory in the context of technological change, deepens the understanding of the mechanism linking technological perception to youth career psychology, and offers practical implications for career guidance in universities.

items.title: AI chatbots showed higher response accuracy than dentists, medical doctors, and the general public on radiation safety questions
items.abstract: Abstract Radiation is encountered in daily life through natural and artificial sources as well as in medical diagnostic and therapeutic applications, and its exposure may lead to adverse health effects. This study aimed to assess radiation-related knowledge among dentists, medical doctors, and the general public and to compare their response accuracy with that of AI-based chatbot systems. A 25-item multiple-choice questionnaire assessing radiation risks and radiation safety was administered to 344 individuals, including dentists, medical doctors, and members of the general public. The same questions were entered into seven selected AI-based chatbot systems (Claude, DeepSeek, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Perplexity AI, ChatGPT-5, and ChatGPT-4o). The response accuracy of the chatbots was compared with that of the human participants. In addition, the consistency of their performance across different users and time periods was comparatively analyzed. AI-based systems generally demonstrated higher accuracy rates compared to human participants. Accuracy rates ranged from 80 to 90.67% among AI-based systems, compared with 32–60% among human participants. Among the evaluated chatbot systems, Microsoft Copilot achieved the highest performance, while Perplexity AI exhibited the lowest. Among the human groups, dentists and medical doctors performed significantly better than the general public, with no significant difference between the two healthcare professional groups. Performance remained stable across morning, midday, and evening assessments for most AI systems; however, ChatGPT-5 showed a significant temporal difference ( p < 0.001). AI-based systems achieved higher response accuracy than human participants under the evaluation conditions used in this study. The overall performance of the human participant groups indicates room for improvement in radiation safety education. While AI-based tools may serve as valuable educational resources, their performance should not be interpreted as evidence of superior clinical judgment or decision-making ability.

items.title: AI DOES NOT JUDGE: EPISTEMIC ARCHAEOLOGY AND GOVERNANCE OF MEANING IN THE HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
items.abstract: The adoption of GenAI in research is reshaping the epistemic conditions of knowledge production. While LLMs are often perceived as neutral agents, this paper argues that the humanities and social sciences (HSS) serve as critical infrastructures for governing AI-mediated inquiry. Drawing on sociotechnical pragmatism, the article introduces epistemic archaeology: an interpretive orientation that treats AI outputs as stratified artifacts shaped by cultural and statistical histories. Rather than seeking validation in convergence, this approach interprets model divergence as signals of training data and epistemic constraints. By foregrounding interpretation, contextualization, and epistemic literacy, the work establishes the foundational coordinates for AI integration. This conceptual positioning preserves human responsibility and judgment as the primary locus of meaning in human–AI interaction. While serving as the theoretical base for future applications, the paper defines the ethical landscape for responsible academic research.

items.title: AI Implications for the Quality of Counselling Practice
items.abstract: Although the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming educational guidance and career counselling, its impact on quality and professionalism has not been sufficiently researched. This scoping review investigates how AI influences counselling methods and professional standards and analyses 20 publications (2015–2025) from two databases (ERIC and German Education Index) using a systematic micro-, meso-, and macro-level framework. Although research in this area has grown rapidly since 2022, concrete quality standards for AI-supported counsel­ling remain elusive. While AI can simulate empathy and provide reflective prompts, it cannot replicate genuine human warmth or address complex biographical issues. Acknowledging AI’s potential to enhance accessibility, it only serves as an expansion of the repertoire rather than a replacement for human reflexivity. In order to safeguard professional integrity in the postdigital era, the study recommends implementing mandatory AI competencies and establishing a digital commons infrastructure to protect counselling values from commercial interests.

items.title: AI IN THE INDIAN JUDICIARY: CAN TECHNOLOGY REDUCE PENDENCY WITHOUT REPLACING HUMAN JUDGMENT?
items.abstract: This article examines the potential of artificial intelligence to reduce judicial pendency in India without compromising human judgment. It explores existing applications, including SUPACE, SUVAS and eCourts Phase III, alongside judicial concerns regarding fabricated citations, algorithmic bias and automation bias. Through an analysis of relevant Indian judicial decisions, the article distinguishes AI-assisted research and administrative functions from adjudicatory decision-making. It argues that AI should complement, rather than replace, judicial reasoning through mandatory human verification, independent assessment of legal authorities and accountable use. The article concludes that responsible integration of AI can improve judicial efficiency while preserving fairness, accuracy and legitimacy.

items.title: AI Integration in Indonesian Education: Trends, Outcomes, and Challenges - A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Background Global education trends show the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the leading technologies worldwide, a shift increasingly reflected in Indonesian education. This study aims to provide a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) by mapping the research landscape, its representation in practice and policy, its impact on learning quality, and the barriers to AI integration in Indonesian education. Method Using the PRISMA protocol, 34 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus and Google Schoolar databases (2020–2026) were systematically selected and thematically analyzed across four main themes. Results The findings indicate a rapid increase in publication productivity, particularly following the worldwide expansion of generative AI technologies after 2022. However, this growth remains unevenly distributed, concentrated in higher education institutions and urban centers on the island of Java, with a marked absence in primary and secondary education levels and in regions outside Java. The majority of AI-driven implementations consist of generative chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and intelligent tutoring systems, alongside emerging applications such as learning analytics and AI-powered instructional media. Several studies included in this review reported that AI has contributed to measurable improvements in student outcomes including learning achievement, motivation, engagement, and teaching efficiency in well-implemented AI environments. Nonetheless, its adoption also poses significant risks, including a decline in students’ critical thinking skills, threats to academic integrity, and the absence of comprehensive data privacy policies and ethical standards governing AI use in education. Conclusion These findings underscore the urgent need for a responsible AI implementation framework in Indonesia one that incorporates standardized AI literacy competencies for teachers, locally contextualized ethical policies, and a functional national roadmap for AI-enabled educational transformation.
